{{Use British English|date=July 2022}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''John Donald Currey''' (9 August 1932 – 18 December 2018), was a British [[zoologist]] who lectured at the [[University of York]] where he specialised in the [[biomechanics]] of [[mineralised tissues]] such as [[bone]].<ref name="Fleck">{{Cite journal |last=Fleck |first=Claudia |date=2019 |title=In memoriam – John D. Currey, 1932–2018 |journal=Journal of Biomechanics |volume=84 |pages=1–3 |doi=10.1016/j.jbiomech.2019.01.028 |via=[[Elsevier]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019|title=Remembering John D Currey 1932-2018|url=https://esbiomech.org/newsletter/esbiomech-newsletter-spring-2019/remembering-john-d-currey-1932-2018/|access-date=6 October 2021|website=European Society of Biomechanics}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019|title=In Memory of John Currey|url=https://yustart.hubbub.net/p/remembering-john-currey/|access-date=6 October 2021|website=York Unlimited}}</ref><ref name="York">{{Cite web|title=Professor John D Currey|url=https://www.york.ac.uk/biology/staff/jdc.htm|access-date=6 October 2021|website=Department of Biology University of York}}</ref><ref name="Williamson">{{cite book|url=https://www.york.ac.uk/media/biology/documents/aboutthedepartment/Department-of-Biology-50thAnniversary-book.pdf|title=A History of the first fifty years of Biology at York|date=2013|publisher=[[University of York]]|editor-last1=Williamson|editor-first1=Mark|location=UK|editor-last2=White|editor-first2=David|access-date=6 October 2021}}</ref>

== Early life ==

He was born in [[Scunthorpe]] in 1932 and later the family moved to [[Pickwick, Wiltshire]]. He went to [[St Edward's School, Oxford]], and completed his [[national service]] before reading [[zoology]] at [[Brasenose College, Oxford]]; he was awarded a "[[British undergraduate degree classification#First-class honours|first]]" in 1956.<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 June 1956 |title=University News |page=10 |work=[[The Times|Times]] |url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/CS169563863/TTDA?u=rtl_ttda&sid=bookmark-TTDA&xid=aeda44e3 |access-date=6 October 2021 |via=The Times Digital Archive}}</ref> After graduation he served as a [[whaling]] inspector in the [[Antarctic]] on board the [[whaling ship]] ''[[Christian Salvesen|Southern Harvester]]''.<ref name="Fleck"/>

== Career ==

He worked as a demonstrator in the zoology department at [[Department of Zoology, University of Oxford|Oxford]] and completed his D. Phil. in 1961; the title of his thesis was "Functional aspects of the structure of bone, with special reference to Haversian systems".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.711077 |title=EThOS: e-theses online service |publisher=British Library |access-date=16 April 2023 |archive-date=16 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416211131/https://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.711077 }}</ref> He moved to the new [[Department of Biology, University of York|biology department at York University]] in 1964. He spent a year in 1969 at the Veterans Administration Hospital and [[Case Western Reserve University]], [[Cleveland]], USA. In 1970, he returned to York as a professor. Although his main area of research was the mechanics of bone, he spent some years studying the polymorphism of shell colouration in ''[[Cepaea]]'' snails, particularly in collaboration with [[Arthur Cain]].<ref>{{Cite news|date=29 May 1968|title=Snail shells reflect changes in climate|page=16|work=Times|url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/CS269446845/TTDA?u=rtl_ttda&sid=bookmark-TTDA&xid=751b5d4a|access-date=6 October 2021|via=The Times Digital Archive}}</ref> He investigated bone and other hard tissues from a particularly diverse range of vertebrates (e.g. [[narwhal tusk]], crocodile nasal bone and whale [[Auditory bulla|bulla]]),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Currey |first1=J.D. |title=The design of mineralised hard tissues for their mechanical functions |journal=Journal of Experimental Biology |date=1999 |volume=202 |issue=23 |pages=3285–3294 |doi=10.1242/jeb.202.23.3285}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Currey |first1=J.D. |last2=Brear |first2=K. |last3=Zioupos |first3=P. |title=Dependence of mechanical properties on fibre angle in narwhal tusk, a highly oriented biological composite |journal=Journal of Biomechanics |date=July 1994 |volume=27 |issue=7 |pages=885–897 |doi=10.1016/0021-9290(94)90261-5}}</ref> and a number of his papers dealt with the biomechanics of mollusc shells and other invertebrate skeletons.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Currey |first1=J.D. |title=A comparison of the strength of echinoderm spines and mollusc shells |journal=Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom |date=May 1975 |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=419–424 |doi=10.1017/S0025315400016039}}</ref> He was head of the Department of Biology at York from 1984 to 1990, after which he became [[Deputy Vice Chancellor]]. He retired in 1999 and was named as [[professor emeritus]].<ref name="Fleck"/><ref name="Williamson"/>

He was one of the first to point out that diffuse damage and microcracks can help make the bone stronger. "When bone starts to break thousands of little microcracks form. These microcracks are positioned sensibly in relation to the histological structure of the bone, but we don't know where they form in relation to the ultrastructure. Typically when microcracks form they only reach a few microns in length before they come to a halt. The big question is, what brings them to a halt?".<ref name="York"/>

In 2013 the European Society of Biomechanics awarded him the Huiskes Medal for Biomechanics.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Huiskes Medal for Biomechanics|url=https://esbiomech.org/esb-awards/the-huiskes-medal-for-biomechanics/|access-date=6 October 2021|website=European Society of Biomechanics}}</ref> He authored over one hundred papers, appearing between 1959 and 2020.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burr |first1=David |last2=Zaslansky |first2=Paul |last3=Fleck |first3=Claudia |date=2020 |title=Celebrating John D. Currey's Contributions to the Science of Bone |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/bone/special-issue/10VZ6CMZR77 |journal=[[Bone (journal)|Bone]] |volume=Special issue |access-date=6 October 2021 |via=[[Science Direct]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fleck |first1=C. |last2=Burke |first2=M. |last3=Ganzosch |first3=G. |last4=Müller |first4=C. |last5=Currey |first5=J.D. |last6=Zaslansky |first6=P. |title=Breaking crown dentine in whole teeth: 3D observations of prevalent fracture patterns following overload |journal=Bone |date=1 March 2020 |volume=132 |article-number=115178 |doi=10.1016/j.bone.2019.115178}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=J D Currey's research while affiliated with New York University and other places |url=https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/J-D-Currey-38471512 |access-date=6 October 2021 |website=[[ResearchGate]]}}</ref>

== Personal life ==

He married Jillian Vine in 1960, and they had two boys and a girl. He was a keen and proficient [[orienteering|orienteerer]].<ref name="Fleck"/>

== Books ==

* Animal Skeletons (1970). John D. Currey. Institute of Biology. Studies in biology: no. 22. New York, [[St. Martin's Press]]
*Mechanical Design in Organisms (1982). Stephen A. Wainwright, W. D. Biggs, John D. Currey. [[Princeton University Press]]
* The Mechanical Adaptations of Bones (1984). John D. Currey. Princeton University Press. {{ISBN|978-0691612171}}
* Bones: Structure and Mechanics (2002). John D. Currey. Princeton University Press. {{ISBN|978-0691128047}}
